Let’s dive into Chapter 6: Nurturing Ambition and Redefining Success. So, now that we've talked about building equality and autonomy, what's next? Well, it's all about helping kids—especially girls—dream big and chase their ambitions without feeling like they have to say sorry for it. In so many cultures, the ambition we often celebrate in boys gets brushed aside or even discouraged in girls. Boys are pushed to be bold, to go after what they want, while girls sometimes hear, “Don’t be too much.” Over time, that really shapes the way they see themselves—and what they think they’re allowed to aim for. But what if we flipped the script? Nurturing ambition starts with redefining what success means. Instead of just focusing on straight A’s, trophies, or those high-powered careers, imagine if we celebrated the pursuit of meaningful goals, personal growth, and the positive impact kids can have. When we open up that definition, it gives every child the freedom to explore what truly lights them up—without feeling boxed in by someone else’s idea of “making it.” So, how can caregivers and parents support this? Here are a few ways that really make a difference:
First, celebrate effort, curiosity, and resilience just as much as the final outcome. Next, encourage kids to set their own goals—and to take real pride in every bit of progress, not just the end result. And don’t forget to surround them with all kinds of role models. Share stories of women scientists, male nurses, or nonbinary artists. When kids see people like them breaking barriers, it shows that ambition isn’t tied to gender. Think about the difference when a girl says she wants to be an engineer, or a boy dreams of dancing. If you respond with genuine excitement—and maybe help them find a club or a mentor—you’re telling them loud and clear: your dreams are worth pursuing. Of course, there are still some tough pressures out there—especially for girls. Sometimes, they worry about being called “bossy,” “aggressive,” or “unladylike” if they speak up or take the lead. That can hold them back from raising their hand or going after what they want. Here’s where you can really help. Reframe assertiveness as something positive. Give them simple, strong words to push back against criticism, like, “I’m proud of speaking up for what I believe in.” And remember, ambition isn’t about always winning or being perfect. It’s about finding what excites you, then having the confidence and support to go after it—your own way. When kids grow up in an environment where ambition is nurtured, not pressured or boxed in, they gain a true sense of purpose and agency—skills that’ll stick with them for life.
